1: ## Khuddaka Nikāya ## Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā ## (Volume II) ## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa ## 4. Maṅgala Sutta Vaṇṇanā This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Maṅgala Sutta. What is its origin? In Jambudīpa, at various city gates, rest houses, assembly halls, and so forth, great crowds of people would gather, pay gold, and have various worldly (bāhiraka) stories told, such as the abduction of Sītā. Each story would conclude after four months. One day, in such a gathering, a discussion concerning blessings arose: "What is a blessing? Is a blessing something seen, something heard, or something sensed? Who knows what a blessing is?" Then, a man named Diṭṭhamaṅgalika said: "I know what a blessing is. In the world, what is seen is a blessing. What is seen refers to a visual object (rūpa) considered highly auspicious." To explain: in this world, some person, having risen early in the morning, sees a cātaka bird, or a bael stick, or a pregnant woman, or young boys well-adorned, or a full pot, or fresh red fish, or a thoroughbred horse, or a thoroughbred carriage, or a bull, or a cow, or a brown cow, or any other such visual object considered highly auspicious. This is called "Diṭṭhamaṅgala" (the blessing of the seen). Some accepted his words, while others did not. Those who did not accept them argued with him.
2:
Then a man named Sutamaṅgalika said: "Sirs, this eye sees both the clean and the unclean, the beautiful and the unbeautiful, the pleasant and the unpleasant. If what is seen by it were a blessing, then everything would be a blessing. Therefore, what is seen is not a blessing. Rather, what is heard is a blessing. What is heard refers to a sound regarded as highly auspicious. For instance, a person here, having risen early, hears such words as 'increased,' or 'increasing,' or 'full,' or 'Phussa [constellation],' or 'delightful,' or 'glory,' or 'increase of glory,' or 'today is a good constellation, a good moment, a good day, a good blessing,' or whatever other such sound regarded as highly auspicious. This is called a 'blessing of the heard' (sutamaṅgala)." Some accepted his words, while others did not. Those who did not accept them argued with him.

Then a man named Mutamaṅgalika said: "Sirs, this ear also hears both the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant. If what is heard by it were a blessing, then everything would be a blessing. Therefore, what is heard is not a blessing. Rather, what is sensed is a blessing. What is sensed refers to an odor, a taste, or a tangible object regarded as highly auspicious. For instance, a person here, having risen early, smells the scent of flowers such as the paduma lotus, or uses a tooth-stick of pleasant touch, or touches the earth, or touches green crops, moist cow dung, a tortoise, a sesame cart, flowers, or fruits, or anoints himself well with clay of pleasant touch, or wears a cloth of pleasant touch, or wears a turban of pleasant touch. Or he performs the act of smelling an odor, tasting a flavor, or touching a tangible object of such a nature regarded as highly auspicious. This is called a 'blessing of the sensed' (mutamaṅgala)." Some accepted his words, while others did not.

Among them, Diṭṭhamaṅgalika was unable to convince Sutamaṅgalika and Mutamaṅgalika. Nor could any one of them convince the other two. Among those people, those who accepted the words of Diṭṭhamaṅgalika held the view: "Only what is seen is a blessing." Those who accepted the words of Sutamaṅgalika and Mutamaṅgalika held the view: "Only what is heard, only what is sensed is a blessing." Thus, this discussion on blessings became well-known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

Then the people throughout the whole of Jambudīpa formed groups and pondered over blessings, asking, "What indeed is a blessing?" The guardian deities of those people, having heard that talk, likewise pondered over blessings. The terrestrial deities (bhummā devā) were friends with those deities; having heard from them, the terrestrial deities also likewise pondered over blessings. The sky deities (ākāsaṭṭha devā) were friends with those deities, and the deities of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājikā devā) were friends with the sky deities. By this means...
3:
The Akaniṭṭha devas, who are friends of the Sudassī devas, also heard the news from them and, in the same manner, gathered in groups to contemplate on what constitutes a blessing (maṅgala). Thus, throughout the ten thousand world systems, the contemplation of blessings arose in all places. Although this contemplation of blessings arose and they deliberated, saying, "This is a blessing, that is a blessing," it remained without a final conclusion for twelve years. Excluding the noble disciples (ariya-sāvakas), all humans, devas, and Brahmas were divided into three groups based on the power of what is seen (diṭṭha), heard (suta), and sensed (muta). Not even a single person was able to reach a final conclusion according to the truth, thinking, "This alone is the blessing." Thus, the uproar concerning blessings (maṅgala-kolāhala) arose in the world.

There are five kinds of uproars (kolāhala): the uproar of the aeon (kappa-kolāhala), the uproar of the universal monarch (cakkavatti-kolāhala), the uproar of the Buddha (buddha-kolāhala), the uproar of blessings (maṅgala-kolāhala), and the uproar of sagehood (moneyya-kolāhala). Among these five, the devas of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), with their hair let down and disheveled, with weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, wearing red garments and assuming a very unsightly appearance, wander along the paths of humans and announce: "O friends, at the end of one hundred thousand years, the destruction of the aeon will occur. This great world will perish, the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be burnt up and destroyed; the destruction of the world will reach as far as the Brahma realm. O friends, develop loving-kindness (mettā); develop compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā). O friends, serve your mother, serve your father, respect the elders in the family, be vigilant, and do not be negligent." This is called the uproar of the aeon (kappa-kolāhala).

The kāmāvacara devas themselves wander along the paths of humans and announce: "At the end of one hundred years, a universal monarch (cakkavatti) will appear in the world." This is called the uproar of the universal monarch (cakkavatti-kolāhala).

The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, however, adorned with the ornaments of Brahmas, wearing Brahma turbans on their heads, filled with joy and happiness, and proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha, wander along the paths of humans and announce: "At the end of one thousand years, a Buddha will appear in the world." This is called the uproar of the Buddha (buddha-kolāhala).

The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas themselves, knowing the thoughts of humans, wander along the paths of humans and announce: "At the end of twelve years, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) will teach the Maṅgala Sutta." This is called the uproar of blessings (maṅgala-kolāhala).
4:
The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas themselves wander along the paths of humans and announce: "At the end of seven years, a certain bhikkhu will meet with the Blessed One and ask about the practice of sagehood (moneyya-paṭipadā)." This is called the uproar of sagehood (moneyya-kolāhala). Among these five uproars, this maṅgala-kolāhala arose in the world among devas and humans who were divided into three groups based on seen blessings and so forth.

Then, although they searched and investigated among devas and humans, they did not know what a blessing was. At the end of twelve years, the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa realm gathered together and consulted one another thus: "O friends, just as a householder is superior to the members of the household, a village headman is superior to the villagers, and a king is superior to all people, even so, this Sakka, the Lord of Devas, is our chief and superior in terms of merit, glory, sovereignty, and wisdom; he is the lord of the two deva realms. What if we were to ask Sakka, the Lord of Devas, about this matter?"

They went to Sakka and, having prostrated before Sakka, the Lord of Devas—whose body was radiant with garments and ornaments suitable for that moment, who was surrounded by two and a half koṭis (twenty-five million) of nymphs, and who was seated on the noble Paṇḍukambala stone throne at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree—they stood at a respectful distance and addressed him thus: "O Lord Sakka, please be informed; currently, the problem of blessings has arisen. Some say that seen objects are blessings, some say that heard objects are blessings, and some say that sensed objects are blessings. In this regard, we and others have not yet reached a conclusion. It would be good if you would explain it to us as it truly is."

The king of devas, being naturally wise, asked: "Where did this talk of blessings first arise?" They replied: "Lord, we heard it from the Cātumahārājika devas." From there, it was explained that the Cātumahārājika devas heard it from the Ākāsaṭṭha devas, the Ākāsaṭṭha devas from the Bhumma devas, and the Bhumma devas from the guardian devas of humans. Then the guardian devas of humans said: "It first arose in the human world."

Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas, asked: "Where is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) residing?" They replied: "Lord, He is residing in the human world." He asked: "Has anyone asked that Blessed One yet?" They replied: "Lord, no one has asked Him yet." Sakka said: "O friends, why do you discard a fire and try to light a firefly? Why do you think that I should be asked, bypassing that Blessed One who can teach all blessings without exception? Come, friends, let us go and ask that Blessed One; we will surely obtain a glorious answer to the question." He then commanded a certain young deva (devaputta): "You ask the Blessed One." That young deva...
5:
Adorning himself with ornaments suitable for that moment, shining like a streak of lightning, and surrounded by a host of deities, he came to the Jetavana Mahāvihāra. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and standing at a respectful distance, desiring to ask a question about blessings, he addressed him in verse. The Blessed One, wishing to answer that deity's question, spoke this Maṅgala Sutta.

In this Maṅgala Sutta, the meaning of the words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" has been briefly explained in the commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. Those who desire a detailed explanation should take it according to the method stated in the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī. In the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta, it is said: "He was staying in the Magadha country, at the brahmin village of Ekanāḷā in Dakkhiṇāgiri." In this Maṅgala Sutta, however, it is said: "He was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika." Therefore, starting with this word "Sāvatthiyaṃ," I shall provide the commentary on the words not yet explained here.

To explain it, "Sāvatthiyaṃ" means in the city named Sāvatthī. It is said that this city was the dwelling place of a seer named Savattha. Therefore, just as the dwelling place of the seer Kusamba is called Kosambī, and the dwelling place of the seer Kākaṇḍa is called Kākaṇḍī, so too, it is called "Sāvatthī" in the feminine gender. Ancient teachers, however, explain: because when groups of merchants met in that place and were asked, "What goods (bhaṇḍa) are there (atthi)?" they replied, "Everything is there (sabbaṃ atthi)," it is called "Sāvatthī" based on those words. "In that Sāvatthī" (Sāvatthiyaṃ). By this, his alms-resort village is indicated. Because it was planted and nurtured by the prince named Jeta, it is Jeta's wood, hence "Jetavana"; in that Jetavana. Because he provided alms (piṇḍa) to the helpless (anātha), he is called "Anāthapiṇḍika"; of that Anāthapiṇḍika. It means in the monastery completed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with an expenditure of fifty-four koṭis. By this, his dwelling place suitable for renunciants is indicated.

"Atha" is a particle in the sense of non-interruption. "Kho" is a particle in the sense of indicating another subject. By these, it shows that while the Blessed One was staying in that monastery, without interruption, "this other subject arose." What is that? "Aññatarā devatā" and so on. Among those words, "Aññatarā" is an indefinite designation. Because that deity was not well-known by name or clan, he is called "Aññatarā" (a certain). "Devatā" is simply a deity; this term is common to both female and male. Here, however, he was indeed a male deity (devaputta), but he is called "devatā" by way of the common name.
6:
In the phrase "Abhikkantāya rattiyā," the word "Abhikkanta" is found in the senses of exhaustion (end), goodness, beauty, great rejoicing, and so on. Among these meanings, it is found in the sense of exhaustion (khaya) in such passages as: "Venerable Sir, the night is spent (abhikkantā), the first watch has passed, the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time. May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks." It is found in the sense of goodness (sundara) in such passages as: "This person is more excellent (abhikkantataro) and more sublime than these four persons."

It is found in the sense of beauty (abhirūpa) in such passages as: "Who is it that worships my feet, shining with psychic power and glory, illuminating all directions with surpassing beauty (abhikkantena vaṇṇena)?" It is found in the sense of great rejoicing (abbhanumodanā) in such passages as: "Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent (abhikkantaṃ), Master Gotama!" Here, however, it is in the sense of exhaustion (end). Therefore, "Abhikkantāya rattiyā" means when the first watch of the night had ended.

In the phrase "Abhikkantavaṇṇā," the word "Abhikkanta" is in the sense of beauty, while the word "Vaṇṇa" is found in the senses of complexion, praise, caste, cause, shape, measure, visible object, and so on. Among those meanings, it is found in the sense of complexion (chavi) in such passages as: "The Blessed One is of golden complexion (suvaṇṇavaṇṇo)." It is found in the sense of praise (thuti) in such passages as: "Householder, when did you ever hear these praises (vaṇṇā) of the ascetic Gotama?" It is found in the sense of caste (kulavagga) in such passages as: "Master Gotama, there are these four castes (vaṇṇā)." It is found in the sense of cause (kāraṇa) in such passages as: "If so, for what reason (vaṇṇena) is he called a 'scent-thief'?" It is found in the sense of shape (saṇṭhāna) in such passages as: "Having created the form (vaṇṇaṃ) of a great elephant king." It is found in the sense of measure (pamāṇa) in such passages as: "There are three sizes (vaṇṇā) of alms-bowls." It is found in the sense of visible object (rūpāyatana) in such passages as: "Color (vaṇṇo), odor, taste, and nutritive essence." Here, the word "Vaṇṇa" should be understood in the sense of complexion. Therefore, "Abhikkantavaṇṇā" means one who has a very beautiful complexion.

In the word "Kevalakappa," the word "Kevala" has many meanings such as entire (without remainder), mostly, unmixed, without excess, firm, detached, and so on. Thus, in such passages as "the holy life (brahmacariya) that is entirely (kevala) complete and pure," the meaning is "without remainder." In "all (kevalakappā) the people of Aṅga and Magadha, having taken plenty of food and snacks..."
7:
In the Pali texts such as 'will approach' (Mahāvagga, 43), the word kevala has the meaning of 'mostly'. In texts such as 'it is the origin of the entire mass of suffering' (Vibhaṅga, 225), it has the meaning of 'unmixed'. In texts such as 'this venerable one has only a measure of faith' (Mahāvagga, 244), it has the meaning of 'not exceeding'. In texts such as 'Venerable, a co-resident of Venerable Anuruddha named Bāhika has stood for a whole eon for the sake of schism in the Saṅgha' (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 4.243), it has the meaning of 'firmness'. In texts such as 'one who is absolute, who has lived the life, is called a supreme person' (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 3.57), it has the meaning of 'disconnection' (from defilements). In this context, however, the intended meaning of the word kevala is 'without remainder' (entire).

The word kappa also has many meanings such as great faith, usage, time, designation, cutting, specific thought, hint, and pervading all around. Thus, in texts such as 'this word of the Master Gotama is very much to be believed' (Majjhima Nikāya, 1.387), it has the meaning of 'great faith'. In texts such as 'Monks, I allow you to enjoy fruit by five kinds of ascetic usage' (Cuḷavagga, 250), it has the meaning of 'usage'. In texts such as 'by which way I dwell for a constant time' (Majjhima Nikāya, 1.387), it has the meaning of 'time'. In texts such as 'thus Venerable Kappa' (Sutta Nipāta, 1098), it has the meaning of 'designation'. In texts such as 'adorned with hair and beard that have been cut' (Jātaka, 2.22), it has the meaning of 'cutting'. In texts such as 'the two-finger-breadth rule is allowable' (Cuḷavagga, 446), it has the meaning of 'specific thought'. In texts such as 'there is a hint for lying down' (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 8.80), it has the meaning of 'hint'. In texts such as 'having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana all around' (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 1.94), it has the meaning of 'pervading all around'. In this context, the intended meaning of the word kappa is 'pervading all around'. Therefore, in the phrase 'kevalakappaṃ Jetavanaṃ', the meaning should be understood as 'the entire Jetavana, pervading all around without remainder'.

'Obhāsetvā' means having pervaded with radiance, making the whole area have a single radiance and a single light, like the moon or the sun.

In the sentence 'yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami', the instrumental case (yena, tena) is used in the sense of location (bhūmma). Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'where the Blessed One was, there he approached'. Alternatively, it can be understood as 'for whatever reason the deities and humans should approach the Blessed One, for that very reason he approached'. For what reason should one approach the Blessed One? One should approach with the desire to attain various kinds of special virtues, just as flocks of birds approach a great tree that is always fruiting with the desire to enjoy the delicious fruit. 'Upasaṅkami' means...
8:
...means having reached the act of approaching. The word 'upasaṅkamitvā' indicates the completion of the approach. Alternatively, it means having arrived and gone to a very close place, which is called the vicinity of the Blessed One. 'Bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā' means having paid homage, bowed, and shown reverence to the Blessed One.

'Ekamantaṃ' is a neuter designation indicating a state, meaning 'at one spot' or 'to one side'. Alternatively, it is the use of the accusative case in the sense of the locative (place). 'Aṭṭhāsi' means having rejected postures such as sitting and performing the act of standing; it means 'remained standing'.

As to how that deity stood 'at one side':
"Not directly behind, nor directly in front,
Nor too close, nor too far,
Not to the side, nor against the wind,
Nor too low, nor too high;
Avoiding these faults, she stood at one side."

Why did that deity only stand and not sit? Because of the desire to return quickly. Indeed, deities come to the human world only for some specific purpose, just as a clean person goes to a cesspool. By nature, from a hundred yojanas away, the human world is repulsive to deities because of its foul smell; they do not delight in it. Therefore, that deity did not sit because she wanted to return quickly after performing the task for which she came. Alternatively, while people usually sit to relieve the fatigue of postures like walking, deities do not have such fatigue; for this reason also, she did not sit. She also did not sit out of respect for the great disciples who stood surrounding the Blessed One. Furthermore, she did not sit solely out of respect for the Blessed One. Indeed, for deities who wish to sit, a seat appears automatically, but not desiring it, she did not even form the thought of sitting and stood at one side.

'Ekamantaṃ ဌိတာ khေါ sā devatā' means 'that deity who, for these reasons, stood at one side'. 'Bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi' means she addressed the Blessed One with a verse composed of syllables and words.

In that verse, 'bahū' is a designation of an indefinite number. Therefore, it means many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands. 'Devā' means those who play with the five kinds of sensual pleasures, or those who shine with their own glory. Furthermore, there are three kinds of deities: conventional deities (sammuti-deva), deities by rebirth (upapatti-deva), and deities by purity (visuddhi-deva). Regarding this...
9:
Regarding the term "Devā," there are three types of deities: conventional deities (sammuti-devā), deities by rebirth (upapatti-devā), and deities by purity (visuddhi-devā). Among them, conventional deities refer to kings, queens, and princes. Deities by rebirth refer to those starting from the Cātumahārājikā realm and the higher celestial realms. Deities by purity refer to the Arahants.

Among these three types of deities, the deities by rebirth (upapatti-devā) are intended here. They are called "manussa" (humans) because they are the descendants of Manu. However, ancient teachers say they are called "manussa" because of the loftiness of their minds. These humans are of four types: those of Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha. In this context, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa are intended. They are called "maṅgala" (blessings) because through these qualities, beings attain prosperity and growth. It means they reach fulfillment and increase. "Acintayuṃ" means they have pondered. "Ākaṅkhamānā" means desiring, longing, or yearning. "Sotthānaṃ" refers to the state of well-being. It means the presence of beautiful, good, and wholesome qualities in both the present life and future existences. "Brūhi" means preach, show, tell, reveal, analyze, and make clear. "Maṅgalaṃ" is the cause of fulfillment, the cause of growth, and the cause of all success (sampatti). "Uttamaṃ" means distinguished, noble, and that which brings welfare and happiness to the whole world. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā) of the verse.

This is the summarized meaning (piṇḍattha): That deity saw that the deities from ten thousand world systems, desiring to hear the question on blessings, had gathered in this single world system. Even in a space as small as the tip of a single hair, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or eighty deities had created subtle forms for themselves. Seeing the Blessed One surrounded by all the devas, Māras, and Brahmās, outshining them with glory and power, and seated upon the prepared noble Buddha-seat; and at that time, knowing with his own mind the thoughts of all the humans of Jambudīpa who had not yet arrived, and for the purpose of uprooting the thorn of doubt of all devas and humans, he spoke thus: "Many devas and humans, desiring their own well-being, have pondered upon blessings. At the request of those devas and out of a desire to favor humans, I ask: please, Blessed One, out of compassion for us, preach the supreme blessing which can truly bring welfare and happiness to all of us."
10:
Having heard the words of the deity in this manner, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ." In that verse, "asevanā" means non-association, not attending upon. "Bālānaṃ" (of fools): they are called "bāla" because they merely breathe (balanti); the meaning is that they live only by inhaling and exhaling, not by the life of wisdom. (It refers to the non-association with) those fools. "Paṇḍitānaṃ" (of the wise): they are called "paṇḍita" because they are wise/clever; the meaning is that they move with the gait of knowledge regarding benefits in the present and the future. (It refers to the association with) those wise ones. "Sevanā" means associating, attending upon with humility, being a companion to that person, and inclining towards that person. "Pūjā" means showing respect, honoring, revering, and saluting. "Pūjaneyyānaṃ" means (honoring) those worthy of honor. "Etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ": combining all these—the non-association with fools, the association with the wise, and the honoring of those worthy of honor—He said, "This is the supreme blessing." In response to what you, the deity, asked, "Preach the supreme blessing," it means: "First, take these (three) as the supreme blessing." This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā) of this verse.

As for the commentary on the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā), it should be understood thus: Having heard the words of the deity in this manner, the Blessed One spoke this verse. In this regard, there are four types of discourse (kathā): discourse spoken because of another's question (pucchitakathā), discourse spoken of one's own accord without being asked (apucchitakathā), discourse with a sequential connection (sānusandhikathā), and discourse without a sequential connection (ananusandhikathā). Among these four, discourses preached because of another's question, such as "I ask you, Gotama, who are possessed of broad wisdom, what must a disciple do to be good?" and "Friend, how did you cross the flood?", are called "pucchitakathā." Discourses preached by one's own intention (attajjhāsaya) without being asked by others, such as "What others call happiness, the Noble Ones call suffering," are called "apucchitakathā." All the words of the Buddhas are discourses with sequential connection (sānusandhikathā), according to the statement: "Monks, I preach the Dhamma with a cause/reason." There is no discourse without sequential connection (ananusandhikathā) in this Dispensation. Among such discourses, this (Maṅgala Sutta) is a "pucchitakathā" because it was preached by the Blessed One as asked by the deity.

In preaching a pucchitakathā, just as a man skilled in paths, knowing the right path and the wrong path, first tells a person asking for the way which path to avoid and then tells which path to take—saying, "At such and such a place, there is a fork in the road; there, leave the left and take the right"—so too, among those to be associated with and those not to be associated with, He first mentions those not to be associated with and then mentions those to be associated with. The Blessed One is like the man skilled in paths. As He said: "Tissa, 'a man skilled in paths' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One."
11:
The Blessed One is skilled in this world, skilled in the world beyond, skilled in the realm of death, skilled in the realm of non-death, skilled in the realm of Māra, and skilled in the realm of non-Māra. Therefore, wishing to speak first of those who should not be associated with and then of those who should be associated with, he said: "Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise." Indeed, just like a path to be abandoned, first, fools should not be associated with or attended to; then, like a path to be taken, the wise should be associated with and attended to.

Why did the Blessed One, when teaching the Mangala Dhamma, first teach the non-association with fools and the association with the wise? The answer is stated: Because gods and humans, through association with fools, held this view of "auspiciousness" in things seen and so forth, and that view is inauspicious. Therefore, the Blessed One taught the non-association with fools and the association with the wise first, by way of censuring the association with bad friends (akalyāṇamitta) which destroys the welfare of this life and the next, and by way of praising the association with good friends (kalyāṇamitta) which accomplishes the welfare of both worlds.

In that context, those called "fools" (bāla) are any beings endowed with unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha) such as killing living beings. Those fools are to be known by three characteristics. As it is taught in the Sutta: "Monks, these three are the fool's characteristics of a fool." Furthermore, the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, as well as Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodaka Tissa, Khaṇḍadeviyāputta, Samuddadatta, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and in the past, the brother of Dīghavida—these and other such beings are to be known as fools.

Like a glowing ember, those fools destroy themselves and those who follow their words through the wrong views they have wrongly grasped. For example, the brother of Dīghavida, with a body measuring sixty yojanas, fell flat and suffered in the Great Hell for the interval between four Buddhas; likewise, the five hundred families who delighted in his view fell into hell along with him and suffered. For it was said:

"Monks, just as a fire released from a reed house or a grass house burns even gabled houses that are plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows closed; even so, monks, whatever..."
12:
"Monks, whatever fears arise, all those arise because of the fool, not because of the wise. Whatever calamities (upaddava) arise... whatever troubles (upasagga) arise... they do not arise because of the wise. Thus, monks, the fool is dangerous, the wise is safe. The fool is calamitous, the wise is free from calamity. The fool is troublesome, the wise is free from trouble," (thus it was taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

Furthermore, a fool is like a rotten fish; one who associates with that fool is like the leaf-container used to wrap the rotten fish. Such a person becomes an object of rejection and loathing for the wise. And it was said:

"When a man wraps rotten fish with kusa grass,
the kusa grass also smells of rot;
such is the association with fools."

Akitti the Wise (Akitti Paṇḍita) also said this when Sakka, the King of the Gods, offered him a boon:

"I would not see a fool, nor hear a fool, nor live with a fool.
I would not converse with a fool, nor take pleasure in a fool."

"Kassapa, what has the fool done to you? Tell me the reason.
Kassapa, why do you not desire to see a fool?"

"The unwise leads to ruin, he engages in what is not one's duty.
He thinks even wrong guidance is excellent; when well-advised, he becomes angry.
He does not know discipline (Vinaya); it is truly best not to see him."

In this way, the Blessed One, censuring the association with fools in every way, said "Not associating with fools is a blessing," and now, wishing to praise the association with the wise, he said "And associating with the wise is a blessing." In that context, the "wise" (paṇḍita) refers to any beings endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) such as abstaining from killing living beings. Those wise persons are to be known by three characteristics. As it was said: "Monks, these three are the wise man's characteristics of a wise man." Furthermore, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty Great Disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata, as well as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma, Nimirājā, Ayoghara Kumāra, Akitti Paṇḍita, and others, are to be known as the wise.
13:
These wise ones are like a protection in times of fear, like a lamp in the darkness, and like the obtaining of food and drink when oppressed by the suffering of hunger and thirst; they are capable of destroying all fears, calamities, and obstacles for those who follow their words. Accordingly, depending on the Tathāgata, countless and immeasurable devas and humans have attained the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), have been established in the Brahma realms, have been established in the deva realms, and have been reborn in the happy destinations (sugati). By gladdening their hearts toward the Elder Sāriputta and serving the Elder with the four requisites, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven. Likewise, it was so with all the great disciples such as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and the Elder Mahākassapa. Among the disciples of the teacher Sunetta, some were reborn in the Brahma realm, some in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas... and some were reborn in the company of wealthy householder families (mahasāla).

And it is said:
'Monks, there is no fear originating from the wise, there is no calamity originating from the wise, there is no obstacle originating from the wise' (Aṅguttara Nikāya).

Furthermore, the wise person is like a fragrant substance such as a Tagara garland. One who associates with that wise person is like the leaf used to wrap that fragrant substance. Such a person becomes one praised by the wise and becomes pleasing to them. Regarding this matter, it is said:
'When a person wraps Tagara flowers with a palāsa leaf,
the leaves also breathe forth a fragrant scent;
such is the association with the wise.'

Akitti the Wise also spoke thus when Sakka, the lord of devas, offered him a boon:
'May I see the wise, may I hear the wise, may I live together with the wise,
may I engage in conversation with the wise, and may I delight in the words of the wise.'

'Kassapa, what has the wise one ever done for you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa, why do you long to see the wise?'

'The wise one leads one to the path of benefit, and does not engage one in what is not beneficial.
Only good guidance is noble; even when spoken to or admonished rightly, the wise one does not get angry.
The wise one knows the discipline (vinaya); therefore, association with the wise is truly excellent.'

In this way, the Blessed One, praising the association with the wise in every manner, declared that associating with the wise is a 'blessing' (maṅgala). Now, regarding the non-association with fools...
14:
Desiring to praise the honoring of those who have gradually reached the state of being worthy of honor through association with the wise, the Blessed One said: 'Honoring those worthy of honor; this is the highest blessing.' In that verse, those 'worthy of honor' (pūjaneyya) are the Blessed Buddhas, because they are free from all faults and endowed with all virtues; after them, the Paccekabuddhas and the Noble Disciples (ariyasāvaka). Honoring these noble ones, even if only slightly, leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. Sumana the florist and Queen Mallikā, among others, are examples of this.

Let us relate just one such example. It is said that one day in the morning, the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. At 그hat time, Sumana the florist, while going to carry flowers for King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, saw the Blessed One who had reached the city gate—graceful, inspiring confidence, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, and shining with the glory of a Buddha. Seeing him, this thought occurred to the florist: 'The King might take these flowers and give me a hundred or a thousand coins, but that benefit would be happiness only in this life. However, honoring the Blessed One has immeasurable and incalculable fruits and brings welfare and happiness for a long time. Let me honor the Blessed One with these flowers.' With a heart full of faith, he took a handful of flowers and threw them toward the Blessed One. The flowers went through the air and remained as a floral canopy above the Blessed One. Seeing that miracle, the florist, with even greater faith, threw another handful of flowers, which went and remained as a floral robe (mañjuka). In this way, he threw eight handfuls of flowers, and they went and remained as a flower mansion (pupphakuṭāgāra).

The Blessed One appeared as if he were inside the flower mansion, and a great crowd of people gathered. The Blessed One, looking at the florist, manifested a smile. The Elder Ānanda, thinking 'Buddhas do not smile without a cause or reason,' asked the reason for the smile. The Blessed One said: 'Ānanda, because of the power of this offering, this florist, after wandering among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, will finally become a Paccekabuddha named Sumanissara.' At the conclusion of his words, he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma:

'That deed is well done which, being done, one does not regret,
and the fruit of which one experiences with a delighted and happy mind.'

At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the Dhamma. Thus, honoring those noble ones, even if only slightly, leads to welfare for a long time.
15:
Seeing that wonderful phenomenon and having a mind full of devotion, he threw another handful of flowers. Those flowers flew up and remained as a floral cluster. In this way, he threw eight handfuls of flowers, and they flew through the air to form a floral canopy. The Blessed One stood as if inside a floral house. A great crowd gathered. The Blessed One, seeing Sumana the florist, manifested a clear smile. The Elder Ānanda, thinking, "Buddhas do not smile without a cause," asked the reason for the smile. The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, because of the power of this offering of flowers, this Sumana the florist, after wandering through the worlds of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, will finally become a Paccekabuddha named Sumana-issara." At the end of the discourse, for the sake of the Dhamma teaching, He spoke this verse: "Where Sumana the florist threw flowers as an offering to the Blessed One, that Blessed One accepted them. That deed of making an offering of flowers, performed without regret, is indeed excellent."

At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths. Thus, it should be understood that even a small offering to the Buddhas leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. That offering was merely a material offering (āmisapūjā); what then need be said of the offering through practice (paṭipattipūjā)? Those clansmen who honor the Blessed One with their own virtues, such as taking refuge (saraṇagamana), undertaking the precepts (sikkhāpada), observing the Uposatha, and the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla)—who can exhaust the praise of the benefits of their honoring? It is said that they honor the Tathāgata with the highest honor. As the Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, whatever monk, nun, lay follower, or female lay follower lives practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipanna), practicing properly, and conducting themselves according to the Dhamma—such a person respects, reveres, venerates, honors, and pays homage to the Tathāgata with the highest honor."

In this same way, it should be understood that honoring Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) also brings welfare and happiness.

Furthermore, among laypeople, a younger brother should honor an elder brother or sister; a son should honor his parents; and daughters-in-law should honor their husbands and parents-in-law. Thus, those worthy of honor should be recognized. Honoring them is also a blessing (maṅgala), because it is a wholesome deed (kusala) and a cause for the increase of life and other benefits. As it was said:

"They will be those who act rightly toward their mothers and fathers, rightly toward recluses and brahmins, and who respect the elders in the family. They will live undertaking this wholesome Dhamma. By reason of undertaking these wholesome Dhammas, they will increase in life and beauty."

Thus, in this verse, the three blessings—not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor—have been spoken. Among them, not associating with fools is a blessing because it protects against dangers arising from associating with fools and is a cause for the welfare of both worlds. Associating with the wise and honoring those worthy of honor are also to be understood as blessings because they are causes for heaven and Nibbāna, as explained in the account of Sumana. From here on, without showing the table of contents separately, I shall define which blessing exists in which place and clarify its nature as a blessing.

## The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ" is finished.
16:
Thus, although the Blessed One was requested by the deity for only one blessing, saying "Tell me the supreme blessing," like a noble person who gives much when asked for little, He spoke three blessings in one verse. Furthermore, because of the deities' desire to hear, because the blessings exist, and because of the desire to engage various beings in the blessings suitable for them, He began to speak many more blessings with the verses beginning with "Pati-rūpa-desa-vāso ca."

Among those verses, in the first verse, "Pati-rūpa" means suitable or appropriate. "Desa" refers to a village, market town, city, or province—any place where beings reside. "Vāsa" means living in that place. "Pubbe" means in the past, in previous births. "Kata-puññatā" means the state of having accumulated merit. "Atta" refers to the mind, or it refers to the entire personality (attabhāva). "Sammā-paṇidhi" means the right directing or constant application of that self (or mind). The remaining words are as previously explained. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā) here.

The explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā) should be understood as follows: A "suitable locality" (pati-rūpa-desa) is a place where the fourfold assembly (catasso parisā) resides, where bases of meritorious action (puṇṇakiriyavatthu) such as giving occur, and where the ninefold teaching of the Teacher (navaṅga-satthu-sāsana) shines. Living in such a place is called a "blessing" because it is a condition for beings to perform meritorious deeds. The fishermen and others who entered the island of Lankā (Sīhaḷadīpa) are examples here.

Another way: A "suitable locality" refers to the place of the Blessed One's seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), the place where the Wheel of Dhamma was first turned, the place at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree where He performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) and defeated the views of all heretics in the midst of an assembly twelve leagues wide, the place of the descent from the deva world, or any other place where the Buddha and others resided, such as Sāvatthī and Rājagaha. Living in those places is called a "blessing" because it is a condition for beings to obtain the six unsurpassables (cha-anuttariya).

Another way: In the eastern direction is the market town named Kajaṅgala, to its west is Mahāsālā, and beyond that are the bordering regions (paccantajanapada); this side (the interior) is the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). In the south-eastern direction is the river named Sallavatī, beyond which are the bordering regions; this side is the Middle Country. In the southern direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika, beyond which are the bordering regions; this side is the Middle Country. In the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūna, beyond which are the bordering regions; this side is the Middle Country. In the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja, beyond which are the bordering regions...
17:
Patirūpadesa (A Suitable Locality) refers to a place where the fourfold assembly resides, where meritorious actions (puññakiriyavatthu) such as generosity (dāna) occur, and where the ninefold Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha shines. Living in such a place is called a blessing (maṅgala) because it is a cause for the performance of wholesome merit for beings. The fishermen and others who arrived at the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) serve as evidence of this. Alternatively, the area of the Buddha's Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), the place where the First Sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) was preached, the site of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree (Kaṇḍambarukkhamūla) where the Buddha performed miracles and defeated the views of heretics in the midst of an assembly spanning twelve leagues, the city of Saṅkassa where he descended from the celestial realm, and all places where the Buddha resided, such as Sāvatthī and Rājagaha, are known as Patirūpadesa. Living in these places is called a blessing because it enables beings to attain the six incomparable supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma).

Alternatively (according to the Vinaya Mahāvagga), the town of Kajaṅgala to the east, and beyond that the region of Mahāsālā; the river Sallavatī to the southeast; the town of Setakaṇṇika to the south; the brahmin village of Thūṇa to the west; and the mountain Usīraddhaja to the north—the interior of these boundaries (the Middle Country or Majjhimadesa) is called Patirūpadesa. This Middle Country is three hundred leagues in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred in circumference. In this region, Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) who rule over the four great continents and two thousand small islands appear. Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) like Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna appear after fulfilling perfections (pāramī) for one asaṅkheyya and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa). Private Buddhas (Paccekabuddha) appear after fulfilling perfections for two asaṅkheyya and a hundred thousand aeons. Fully Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddha) also appear after fulfilling perfections for four, eight, or sixteen asaṅkheyya and a hundred thousand aeons. In that region, beings follow the advice of the Universal Monarch, establish themselves in the five precepts (pañcasīla), and are destined for the celestial realms. Likewise, by establishing themselves in the advice of Private Buddhas, they are destined for the celestial realms. Those who establish themselves in the advice of the disciples of the Fully Enlightened Buddha are destined for both the celestial realms and Nibbāna. Therefore, living in such a place is called a "blessing" because it is the cause for these attainments.

Pubbe ca katapuññatā (Having performed merit in the past) means having accumulated wholesome merit in past lives in relation to Buddhas, Private Buddhas, and Arahants. This is also called a blessing. Why? Because by seeing Buddhas or Private Buddhas in person, or by hearing even a single four-line verse from the Buddha or his disciples, one can reach the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) at the end of the verse. A person who has performed great deeds (adhikāra) in previous lives and has strong wholesome roots (kusalāmūla) can, through those wholesome roots, develop insight (vipassanā) and reach the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya), like King Mahākappina and his Chief Queen. Therefore, it is said, "Pubbe ca katapuññatā maṅgalaṃ."

Attasammāpaṇidhi (Right self-direction) means, in this world, a person establishing their immoral self in virtue (sīla), establishing a faithless self in the accomplishment of faith (saddhā), and establishing a stingy self in the accomplishment of generosity (cāga). This is called attasammāpaṇidhi. This is also a blessing. Why? Because it leads to the abandonment of dangers in both the present life and future lives, and to the attainment of various benefits.
18:
Thus, in this verse as well, only these three blessings are mentioned: Patirūpadesavāsa, Pubbe ca katapuññatā, and Attasammāpaṇidhi. The reason why these are blessings has already been explained in the respective sections of the verse.

## The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Patirūpadesavāso ca" is finished.

Now, in the verse beginning with "Bāhusaccañca": "Bāhusaccaṃ" means the state of being one who has heard and learned much. "Sippaṃ" means skill in any kind of handicraft or art. "Vinayo" means the discipline of body, speech, and mind. "Susikkhito" means well-trained or well-learned. "Subhāsitā" means well-spoken. The word "yā" is an indefinite pronoun. "Vācā" means speech or utterance. The rest is as previously explained. This is the word-by-word explanation (padavaṇṇanā) in this verse.

The explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā) should be understood as follows: Bāhusaccaṃ is praised as the state of upholding the Teacher's Dispensation, as in: "He is a bearer of what he has heard, a storer of what he has heard," and "Monks, in this Dispensation, a certain person has much learning: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, and so on." This bāhusaccaṃ is called a "blessing" because it is the cause for abandoning unwholesome states and attaining wholesome states, and for the gradual realization of the Ultimate Truth (paramatthasacca). For the Blessed One said:

"Monks, the learned noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity."

It is also stated in another discourse:

"He examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered. When he examines the meaning, the teachings gain his reflective acceptance. When there is reflective acceptance of the teachings, desire (to practice) arises. When desire has arisen, he exerts effort. Exerting effort, he scrutinizes. Scrutinizing, he strives. Striving, he realizes the Ultimate Truth with his own body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom."

Furthermore, even the great learning of laypeople, if it is blameless, should be understood as a "blessing" because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.
20:
For that well-spoken speech, like living in a suitable locality, is called a "blessing" because it is a condition for beings to attain the benefit and happiness of both worlds and Nibbāna. And it was said:
"The speech that the Buddha speaks,
Which is secure for the attainment of Nibbāna
And for making an end of suffering,
That indeed is the most excellent of speeches."

Thus, in this verse, four blessings have been stated: great learning, proficiency in art, well-trained discipline, and well-spoken speech. Their nature as blessings has been clearly explained in their respective places.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Bāhusaccañca" is finished.

Now, in the phrases such as "mātāpitu-upaṭṭhānaṃ," "mātāpitu" means mother and father. "Upaṭṭhānaṃ" means supporting or attending to. "Puttānañca dārānañca" means children and wives. "Saṅgaho" means supporting or assisting. "Anākulā" means not confused. "Kammantā" means the works or occupations themselves. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned; this is the word-by-word commentary.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood as follows: "Mother" refers to the female progenitor who gives birth to children; likewise, "father" refers to the male progenitor. "Supporting" (upaṭṭhāna) means rendering assistance by washing the feet, massaging, anointing, and bathing, as well as by providing the four requisites. In such support, parents are of great help to their children, desiring their welfare and being compassionate. Seeing their young children returning from playing outside with bodies covered in dust, they wipe away the dust, kiss their heads, and feel great affection. Even if children were to carry their parents on their heads for a hundred years and serve them, they would not be able to repay the debt of gratitude to their parents. Because those parents are the ones who bring up, nourish, and show this world to their children, and because they are regarded as "Brahmā" and as "First Teachers" (pubbācariya), supporting them brings praise in this life and the happiness of heaven in the life hereafter. Therefore, it is called a "blessing." For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Parents are called 'Brahmā' and 'First Teachers';
They are worthy of offerings from their children, for they are compassionate to their offspring.
Therefore, a wise person should revere and honor them
With food and drink, with clothing and bedding."
21:
"Because of such service as rubbing off the dirt, bathing, and washing the feet of one's mother and father, the wise praise that person even in this very life; and after death, they rejoice in heaven," so it was said.

Another way—supporting parents means performing the five duties such as providing food and maintaining the family lineage. Such action is to be understood as a "blessing" (maṅgala) because it is the cause of welfare in the present life through the five duties such as restraining them from evil. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

"Householder's son, a son should serve his parents, who are the Eastern direction, in five ways: 'Having been supported by them, I will support them; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will manage the inheritance; or I will give offerings to them when they have passed away.' Householder's son, when a son serves his parents in these five ways, the parents show compassion to the son in five ways: they restrain him from evil, establish him in goodness, train him in arts and sciences, provide him with a suitable wife, and hand over the inheritance at the proper time."

Alternatively, a son who supports his parents by inspiring faith in the Triple Gem, by establishing them in virtue, or by leading them to ordination, is the supreme among those who support parents. This support of the parents is a reciprocation of the kindness shown by the parents and is called a "blessing" because it is the foundation for many benefits in both the present and future lives.

In the term "puttadārassa," both sons and daughters are included under the designation "sons" (puttā). "Dārā" refers to any of the twenty kinds of wives. The combination of children and wife is "puttadāra." Supporting (saṅgaha) them means benefiting them through respect and other means. Such action is to be understood as a "blessing" because it is the cause of welfare in the present life, such as having well-organized occupations. The Blessed One, in saying "The Western direction should be known as wife and children," included the children and wife under the term "wife" and said:
22:
"Householder's son, a husband should serve his wife, who is the Western direction, in five ways: (1) by honoring her, (2) by not disparaging her, (3) by being faithful to her, (4) by handing over authority to her, and (5) by providing her with ornaments. Householder's son, when a husband serves his wife in these five ways, the wife shows compassion to her husband in five ways: (1) she performs her duties well, (2) she is hospitable to the attendants, (3) she is faithful to her husband, (4) she protects the wealth he has acquired, and (5) she is skillful and diligent in all her duties." (Dīgha Nikāya, 3.269)

In another way, "saṅgaha" means supporting through righteous giving, pleasant speech, and beneficial conduct. These include: providing provisions on Uposatha days, allowing her to see festivals on festival days, performing auspicious ceremonies on auspicious days, and giving advice and instruction for welfare in this life and the next. Such support is to be understood as a "blessing" because it is the cause of welfare in this life, welfare in the next life, and the cause for being worthy of homage even by the devas. As Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said:
"Those householders who perform merit, are virtuous, are lay followers (upāsakas), and support their wives righteously—I pay homage to them, Mātali." (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 1.264)

"Unconfused occupations" (anākulā kammantā) refers to occupations such as farming, cattle-rearing, and trade that are free from confusion—such as doing things past the proper time, doing inappropriate things, not doing them at all, or doing them negligently—due to knowing the right time, doing what is appropriate, not being lazy, being endowed with energetic effort, and not being destructive. Performing these tasks skillfully, whether by oneself, one's children and wife, or one's servants and workers, is called a "blessing" because it is the cause for obtaining an increase in wealth and grain in this very life. Regarding this, the Blessed One also said:
"One who does what is appropriate, is responsible, and energetic gains wealth." (Sutta Nipāta, 189; Saṃyutta Nikāya, 1.246)

One who is in the habit of sleeping during the day, who destroys energetic effort at night (fearing loss of sleep), and who is constantly intoxicated as a drunkard, is unable to maintain a household.

"It is too cold, it is too hot, it is too late now"—saying thus,
For the young men who abandon their work,
Benefits pass them by.
23:
“He who, in this world, does not regard cold or heat more than a blade of grass, and performs the duties of a man, does not fall away from happiness.” (Dīgha Nikāya 3.253). Also, “To one gathering wealth like a bee gathering nectar, wealth accumulates like a termite mound.” (Dīgha Nikāya 3.265)—and so forth.

In this way, in this verse also, four blessings are stated: supporting mother, supporting father, cherishing wife and children, and unconfused work. Or, by dividing ‘cherishing wife and children’ into two, there are five; or by making ‘supporting parents’ into one, there are three. Their status as blessings has been clarified in various places.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse on supporting mother and father is finished.

Now, regarding the term ‘dānañca’ (and giving): it is called ‘dāna’ because it is given by means of this gift; it means handing over one’s own property to another. Living according to the Dhamma, or living not devoid of the Dhamma, is called ‘dhammacariyā’. Those who are known as ‘these are ours’ are called ‘ñātakā’ (relatives). Actions that are faultless, not blamed, and not censured are called ‘anavajja’. The rest is as previously explained; this is the word-by-word commentary.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood thus: ‘Dāna’ refers to the volition (cetanā) of relinquishing the ten kinds of gifts, such as food, preceded by wisdom and directed towards another, or the non-greed (alobha) associated with that volition. For by non-greed, one hands over that object to another. Therefore, it is said, ‘It is called dāna because it is given by means of this gift.’ That dāna is called a ‘blessing’ because it is the cause for attaining special fruits in the present life and in the future, such as being dear and pleasing to many people. In this regard, suttas such as ‘Sīha, the donor, the master of giving, is dear and pleasing to many people’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.34) should be remembered.

Another way: Dāna is of two kinds: material gift (āmisa-dāna) and the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna). Among them, material gift is as already described. The teaching of the Dhamma, proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One, which leads to the end of suffering in this world and the next and brings happiness, out of a desire for the welfare of others, is called the gift of Dhamma. Of these two kinds of gifts, this gift of Dhamma is supreme. As it is said:
25:
In this way, by this verse, the four blessings—giving, practicing the Dhamma, supporting relatives, and blameless actions—have been spoken. The nature of these as blessings has also been clarified in their respective sections.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Dānañca" is finished.

Now, in the words beginning with "Āratī viratī", "āratī" means refraining (mental aversion). "Viratī" means special refraining, or it is called "viratī" because beings refrain from evil by means of this mental factor. "Pāpā" refers to unwholesome states. Because of the sense of causing intoxication, it is called "majja" (intoxicant); drinking such intoxicants is "majjapāna"; restraint from that drinking of intoxicants is "saṃyama". Non-negligence is "appamāda". "Dhammesu" means in wholesome states. The remaining words are as previously explained. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā).

The commentary on the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā), however, should be understood thus: "Āratī" is the lack of delight in evil by the mind of one who habitually sees danger in it. "Viratī" is the refraining by way of body and speech through the doors of action. This "viratī" is of three kinds: situational abstinence (sampatta-viratī), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-viratī), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-viratī). Among these, when a person, on account of his birth, family, or lineage, refrains from a present object with the thought, "It is not fit for me to kill this living being or take what is not given," etc., this is called "sampatta-viratī". Refraining that occurs by way of undertaking the precepts, from which time the person does not commit killing and so on, is called "samādāna-viratī". The abstinence associated with the Noble Path is called "samuccheda-viratī", from the occurrence of which the five fears and enmities are stilled for the noble disciple. "Pāpa" (evil) refers to the fourfold unwholesome deeds known as "kamma-kilesa" (defilements of action), which are explained in detail as: "Householder's son, killing living beings is a defilement of action, taking what is not given... [pe]... sexual misconduct... [pe]... false speech is a defilement of action."

"Killing living beings, taking what is not given,
False speech is also spoken of,
And going to another's wife—
The wise do not praise these."

These are the four unwholesome states called defilements of action encompassed by this verse; (refraining) from that evil. All these forms of "āratī" and "viratī" are called "blessings" because they are the cause for attaining various special benefits, such as the abandonment of fear and enmity in this life and the next. In this context, suttas such as "Householder's son, the noble disciple refrains from killing living beings" should also be remembered.
26:
"Majjapānā ca saṃyamo" is a term for refraining from drinking fermented and distilled liquors, which is the cause of negligence, as previously mentioned. For the one who drinks intoxicants does not know what is beneficial, does not know the Dhamma, and may even harm his mother; he may harm his father, the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata. In the present life, he meets with blame; in the future life, he reaches a miserable destination (duggati); and in subsequent lives, he reaches madness. However, one who is restrained from drinking intoxicants reaches the stilling of those aforementioned faults and the attainment of qualities opposite to those faults. Therefore, this restraint from drinking intoxicants should be understood as a "blessing".

"Appamādo ca dhammesu" (heedfulness in wholesome states) means: in the cultivation of wholesome states, the opposite of negligence (pamāda)—which is defined as lack of respect, lack of continuity, lack of persistence, sluggishness, giving up desire, laying down the burden, non-cultivation, non-development, not making much of, non-determination, and non-application. In terms of meaning, it should be understood as being never without mindfulness regarding wholesome states. That heedfulness is called a "blessing" because it is the cause for attaining various wholesome states and for attaining the Deathless (Nibbāna). Regarding this heedfulness, the Teacher's instruction should be remembered: "For the heedful, ardent person..." and "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless," and so on.

In this way, by this verse, the three blessings—abstinence from evil, restraint from drinking intoxicants, and heedfulness in wholesome states—have been taught. The nature of these as blessings has also been explained in their respective places.

## The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with "Āratī viratī" is finished.

Now, in the verse beginning with "Gāravo ca", "gāravo" is the state of being respectful toward those worthy of respect. "Nivāto" is having a humble manner. "Santuṭṭhī" is contentment. "Kataññutā" is knowing the gratitude for what has been done (for one). "Kālena" means at the proper time or occasion. "Dhammasavanaṃ" is hearing the Dhamma. The meaning of the remaining words is as previously explained; this is the word-by-word commentary.

The commentary on the meaning should be understood thus: "Gārava" is the act of showing respect, the making of respect, and the state of being respectful toward those worthy of the application of respect, such as the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Tathāgata, teachers, preceptors, parents, elder brothers, elder sisters, and so on, as is appropriate. This "gārava" is a blessing because it is the cause for reaching a happy destination (sugati) and so forth. Therefore, it is said:
27:
"He pays respect to those worthy of respect, honors those worthy of honor, and venerates those worthy of veneration. Because of that kamma, thus fulfilled and thus undertaken, after the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world. If, after the breaking up of the body... he does not reach the heavenly world but comes to the human state, then wherever he is reborn, he is of high birth." Thus it is stated in the Majjhima Nikāya.

The Blessed One also said: "Monks, there are these seven things that prevent decline (aparihāniya dhamma). Which seven? Respect for the Teacher (satthugāravatā), and so forth." Therefore, this respect (gārava) is called a blessing (maṅgala).

Humility (nivāta) means lowliness of mind and lowliness of conduct. A person endowed with such humility has abandoned conceit and suppressed pride; he is like a foot-rag, like a bull with broken horns, or like a snake with its fangs extracted. He is gentle, amiable, and easy to speak with. This is the quality of humility. This humility is called a blessing because it is a cause for obtaining such virtues as having a retinue. The Blessed One also said: "One who is humble in conduct and not stubborn, being of such a nature, gains a retinue," and so forth.

Contentment (santuṭṭhi) means being satisfied with whatever requisites one receives. This contentment is of twelve kinds. Namely: three kinds regarding robes—contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi), contentment according to one's strength (yathābalasantuṭṭhi), and contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi). Likewise, there are three kinds each for alms-food and the other requisites.

To explain the divisions of contentment: Here, in this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it is of good quality or poor quality. He is satisfied with that robe alone; he does not long for another, and even if he receives another, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi) regarding robes. Furthermore, if a monk is ill and, while wearing a heavy robe, he feels weighed down or exhausted, he may exchange it with a compatible monk for a lighter one. Even while sufficing with that lighter robe, he is still considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantuṭṭhi) regarding robes. Another monk may be one who receives excellent requisites. When he receives a costly robe, such as one made of silk, he reflects: "This robe is suitable for elder monks of long standing or for those of great learning." Having given it to them, he himself collects rags from a dustheap or elsewhere, makes them into an outer robe (saṅghāṭi), and wears it. Even so, he is considered content. This is his contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding robes.
28:
In this Dispensation, a monk receives alms-food, whether it is coarse or fine. He is satisfied with that food alone; he does not long for other food, and even if he receives it, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food. Alternatively, a monk may be ill, and by eating coarse food, his illness becomes severe. He gives that food to a compatible monk and, having consumed ghee, honey, milk, and so forth from that monk's hand, he practices the ascetic's Dhamma. Even so, he is considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food. Another monk receives fine alms-food. He thinks: "This alms-food is suitable for elder monks of long standing and for other fellow celibates who cannot manage without fine alms-food." Having given it to them, he himself goes on alms-round and, eating mixed food, continues to develop the ascetic's Dhamma. Even so, he is considered content. This is his contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food.

In this Dispensation, a lodging is assigned to a monk. He is satisfied and content with that assigned lodging; even if another, better lodging becomes available, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging. Alternatively, a monk may be ill, and by staying in a windless lodging, he suffers greatly from ailments such as bile disorders. He gives that lodging to a compatible monk and, staying in a breezy and cool lodging that was assigned to that monk, he practices the ascetic's Dhamma. Even so, he is considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging. Another monk, even when he receives a fine lodging, does not accept it, reflecting: "A fine lodging is a ground for negligence; when sitting there, sloth and torpor overcome one, and when one wakes up after falling asleep, sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) arise." Rejecting it, he stays wherever it may be—in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a leaf hut. Even so, he is considered content. This is his contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives medicine, such as yellow myrobalan (harītaka) or emblic myrobalan (āmalaka). He is satisfied with that medicine alone; he does not long for ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth received by others, and even if he receives them, he does not take them. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites. Alternatively, a monk who is ill needs oil but receives molasses. He gives that molasses to a compatible monk and, having prepared medicine with oil from that monk's hand, he practices the ascetic's Dhamma. Even so, he is considered content. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābalasantuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites. Another monk, in one bowl...
29:
If, while setting aside the medicine of yellow myrobalan soaked in fermented urine, and being offered the four sweet medicines (catumadhura) in a vessel with the words, "Venerable sir, please accept as much as you wish," a monk considers: "The medicine of yellow myrobalan soaked in fermented urine has been praised by the Buddhas and others; I have gone forth depending on this medicine of fermented urine, and I should strive in it for as long as I live" (as stated in the Vinaya Mahāvagga). Even if his illness could be cured by either of the two medicines, if he rejects the four sweet medicines and treats himself with the yellow myrobalan in fermented urine, he is truly one of supreme contentment. This is his "contentment with what is appropriate" (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding the requisite of medicine.

All such various forms of contentment are called Santuṭṭhi (contentment). This contentment should be understood as a "blessing" (maṅgala) because it is the cause for abandoning evil states such as excessive desire, wicked desire, and great greed; because it is a cause for a happy rebirth; because it is a requisite for the Noble Path; and because it is a cause for being free from fear in the four directions. The Blessed One also said: "One who is content with whatever he receives is free from fear in the four directions."

Kataññutā (gratitude) is the state of knowing and repeatedly recollecting a favor done by someone, whether it be small or great. Furthermore, since only meritorious deeds protect beings from sufferings such as hell, they are of great benefit; therefore, the constant recollection of the benefits of those meritorious deeds should also be understood as "Kataññutā." This gratitude is called a "blessing" because it is praised by the virtuous and is a cause for attaining various special qualities. The Blessed One also said: "Monks, these two persons are rare in the world. Which two? One who is the first to do a favor (pubbakārī), and one who is grateful and appreciative (kataññūkatavedī)."

Kālena dhammassavana (hearing the Dhamma at the proper time) refers to hearing the Dhamma to dispel those states when the mind is restless or when it is overcome by any of the thoughts of sensuality and so on. Other teachers say that hearing the Dhamma every five days is "hearing the Dhamma at the proper time." This is as the Venerable Anuruddha said: "Venerable sir, every five days we sit together for the whole night in Dhamma discussion."

Furthermore, the time when one can approach a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) and hear the Dhamma that can dispel one's doubts should also be understood as "hearing the Dhamma at the proper time." As the Blessed One said: "They, from time to time..."
30:
"...approaching, they ask and inquire," and so forth (as stated in the Dīgha Nikāya, Pāthika Vagga, 3.358). This hearing of the Dhamma at the proper time should be understood as a "blessing" because it is a cause for abandoning the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), attaining the four benefits, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), and various other special attainments. 

For it has been said:
"Monks, at whatever time a noble disciple pays attention, applies his mind, concentrates his whole heart, and lends an ear to listen to the Dhamma, at that time the five hindrances do not exist in him" (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Mahā Vagga, 5.219).

And: "Monks, for those who have heard the Dhamma... and have thoroughly penetrated its meaning, four benefits are to be expected" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta, 4.191).

And: "Monks, these four things, when rightly developed and rightly practiced from time to time, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints. Which four? Hearing the Dhamma at the proper time," and so forth (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta, 4.147).

Thus, by this verse, the five blessings of reverence (gārava), humility (nivāta), contentment (santuṭṭhi), gratitude (kataññutā), and hearing the Dhamma at the proper time (kālena dhammassavana) have been taught. The nature of these states as blessings has been clearly explained in their respective places.

## The explanation of the meaning of the verse "Gāravoca nivātoca" is finished.

Now, in the verse beginning with "Khantī ca": patience is "Khantī." One who is easy to speak to because of being amenable to instruction is "suvaca"; the act of such a person is "sovacassa"; the state of being so is "sovacassatā." Because they have calmed their defilements, they are "Samaṇa" (recluses). "Dassana" means seeing or beholding. Discussion about the Dhamma is "Dhammasākacchā." The meanings of the remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained; this is the word-by-word commentary.

The explanation of the meaning should be understood as follows: Khantī refers to patient endurance (adhivāsanakhantī). A monk endowed with this patience remains unperturbed, like the Khantivādī ascetic, as if not hearing those who abuse him with the ten grounds of abuse, or as if not seeing those who harm him by striking or binding.

For it has been said:
"In the past, there was a recluse who taught patience; even though he remained established in that very patience, the King of Kāsi had his limbs severed" (Jātaka Pāḷi, 1.4.51).
31: Or, like the Venerable Puṇṇa Thera, one reflects, "This is a good deed," because there is no further transgression beyond that abuse. To show this meaning, it was said: "If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and threaten me, then I will think: 'These people of Sunāparanta are truly good, they are very good, because they do not strike me with their hands,'" and so forth (M. Ni. 3.396, Saṃ. Ni. 4.88). One who is endowed with such patience is worthy of praise even by the hermits (isīs). The hermit Sarabhaṅga said: "Having slain anger, one never grieves; The hermits praise the abandoning of malice; One should endure the harsh words of all; The virtuous say this patience is supreme." (Jā. 2.17.64). One is also worthy of praise by the devas. As Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said: "Indeed, he who, being strong, is patient with the weak, They call that the supreme patience; The weak must always be patient." (Saṃ. Ni. 1.250-251). One is also worthy of praise by the Buddhas. As the Blessed One said: "He who, without anger, endures abuse, beating, and imprisonment, Whose strength is patience and whose army is strength, Him I call a Brahmin." (Dhp. 399). That patience should be understood as a "Blessing" (Maṅgala) because it is the cause for attaining these praised virtues and other qualities. Sovacassatā (being easy to admonish) means, when being spoken to by fellow practitioners regarding the Dhamma, not falling into distraction, silence, or fault-finding, but instead prioritizing great respect, reverence, and humility, and accepting by saying, "It is well" (Sādhu). This being easy to admonish is called a "Blessing" because it is the cause for receiving advice and instruction from fellow practitioners, and the cause for abandoning faults and attaining virtues.
32: Seeing ascetics (samaṇānaṃ dassanaṃ) means approaching, attending to, constantly recollecting, listening to, and seeing those who have gone forth, whose defilements are calmed, who have cultivated body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and who are endowed with supreme restraint and tranquility. In a lower sequence of teaching, all of these are called "seeing" (dassana). Such seeing should be understood as a "Blessing" (Maṅgala) because it is of great benefit. The Blessed One also said: "Monks, I say that the seeing of those monks is of great benefit," and so forth (Iti. 104). Therefore, a son of good family who desires his own welfare, upon seeing virtuous monks arriving at the door of his house, should honor them with offerings to the best of his ability if offerings are available. If there are no offerings, he should pay homage with the fivefold prostration. If he cannot fulfill that, he should pay respect with joined palms. If even that cannot be fulfilled, he should look upon them well with eyes of affection and a confident mind. Due to the merit based on such seeing, in many thousands of future lives, diseases of the eye, burning sensations, growths, or pustules will not occur. He will obtain eyes endowed with the five beautiful colors, clear and bright like jeweled doors opened in a celestial mansion, and he will be one who obtains all prosperity among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. It is not surprising that a wise human being should experience such successful results due to the merit of seeing ascetics properly performed. For even in the case of animals, the benefits of seeing ascetics generated by mere faith are praised thus: "The owl with round eyes, Who lived long on the Vediyaka Mountain, Happy indeed is this owl (Kosiya), Who sees the Noble Buddha arisen at the proper time. Having clarified his mind in me, And in the unsurpassed Saṅgha of monks, For a hundred thousand aeons, He shall not go to a state of misery. When passing away from the deva world, Urged by his wholesome kamma, He will be one of infinite wisdom, Renowned as 'Somanassa'."
